clinicalPearls: A characteristically postural headache that worsens on sitting or standing and improves on lying flat, developing within a few days of dural puncture
Typically frontal or occipital and may be accompanied by neck stiffness, photophobia, nausea, tinnitus, or hearing changes
Risk is higher with larger-gauge and cutting (rather than pencil-point) needles, younger age, female sex, and after accidental dural puncture during epidural placement
Diagnosis is largely clinical, but a headache lacking postural features or with neurological signs should prompt evaluation for other causes
Initial management is conservative with rest as needed, hydration, simple analgesia, and reassurance, as many cases resolve spontaneously
An epidural blood patch is the definitive treatment for severe or persistent headache and is generally highly effective
Caffeine and other pharmacological measures have limited and temporary benefit compared with a blood patch
Rare but serious complications of intracranial hypotension include subdural haematoma and cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, so atypical or worsening features require imaging
reference.pathophysiology: A persistent hole in the dura allows cerebrospinal fluid to leak into the epidural space faster than it is produced, lowering cerebrospinal fluid volume and pressure. In the upright position, reduced buoyant support causes traction on pain-sensitive intracranial structures such as the meninges and bridging veins, and compensatory cerebral vasodilation may contribute, producing the postural headache. Larger dural defects leak more and cause more severe symptoms. An epidural blood patch works by sealing the defect and raising epidural and cerebrospinal fluid pressure.
additionalDifferentials: Pre-eclampsia or eclampsia in the obstetric patient
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment focusing on the postural nature of the headache
Neurological examination to exclude focal signs
Brain imaging (CT or MRI) when features are atypical, worsening, or accompanied by neurological signs
Investigations for pre-eclampsia in the postpartum patient when relevant
Assessment for infection if fever or meningism is present
redFlags: Loss of the postural component or a headache that becomes constant, suggesting an alternative or serious cause
Focal neurological deficit, seizure, or reduced consciousness suggesting subdural haematoma or venous thrombosis
Fever, neck stiffness, or photophobia raising concern for meningitis
Sudden thunderclap onset or features suggesting subarachnoid haemorrhage
reference.prognosis: Most postdural puncture headaches resolve within days to weeks with conservative care, and a blood patch relieves the majority of severe cases; rare progression to intracranial haemorrhage or venous thrombosis can cause serious morbidity.
pitfalls: Assuming every post-procedure headache is a postdural puncture headache and missing a dangerous cause
Delaying an effective blood patch in severe, disabling headache
Overlooking evolving neurological signs that indicate subdural haematoma or venous sinus thrombosis
Failing to consider pre-eclampsia in a postpartum woman with headache
Relying on caffeine or bed rest alone for persistent severe symptoms
management: Offer conservative first-line care with rest as needed, oral or intravenous rehydration, and simple analgesia such as paracetamol and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
Add symptomatic measures including antiemetics for nausea and caffeine as an adjunct to counter compensatory cerebral vasodilatation
Reassure the patient that many cases settle spontaneously and adopt a stepwise approach before invasive treatment

Perform an autologous epidural blood patch as the definitive treatment for severe or persistent headache, sealing the dural defect and restoring cerebrospinal fluid pressure, and repeat if the first fails
Involve the anaesthetic or pain service early for blood patch and for management of accidental dural puncture

Monitor for atypical or red-flag features (loss of postural character, focal neurological signs, fever, seizures) that warrant brain imaging to exclude intracranial haemorrhage or cerebral venous thrombosis
In the postpartum patient, actively exclude pre-eclampsia and cortical vein thrombosis as alternative causes
